findings.title: Statement#close finalizes the sqlite3_stmt before checking status, leaving a dangling handle on the raising path
findings.rationale: The dangerous operation is reached because the destructive call is evaluated as the CHECK macro argument, so sqlite3_finalize frees the statement before rb_sqlite3_raise inspects the status. rb_raise at exception.c:93 is a non-local longjmp, so the compensating assignment ctx->st = NULL at statement.c:87 never runs. That single skipped store is what converts an error report into a lasting memory-safety defect: the two guards the codebase relies on to prevent use of a closed statement, Statement#closed? at statement.c:101 and REQUIRE_OPEN_STMT at statement.c:3-5, both test ctx->st for NULL, so both pass with a pointer to released memory. I verified by search that statement.c:18 and statement.c:87 are the only assignments to ctx->st in the file and that the GC free function at statement.c:9-13 never touches it, so nothing downstream notices or repairs the stale pointer. The trigger is attacker-reachable and ordinary rather than exotic: sqlite3_finalize returns a non-OK code when the most recent evaluation of the statement failed (/usr/include/sqlite3.h:5290-5295), Statement#step routes only non-ROW/DONE codes to CHECK (statement.c:131-179) so a deferred constraint or busy error persists in the handle, and Database#prepare calls stmt.close from an ensure block during that very unwind (lib/sqlite3/database.rb:86-90). The Ruby layer adds no compensating check, since must_be_open! at lib/sqlite3/statement.rb:140-144 delegates to the same closed? predicate. Severity is MEDIUM rather than HIGH because exploitation beyond a crash requires the application to rescue the exception and then reuse the same Statement object, and because turning the reuse into controlled corruption depends on reoccupying the freed slab. Difficulty is MEDIUM because forcing a deferred-error step and then shaping intervening allocations needs product knowledge and a custom exploit rather than public tooling. Confidence is MEDIUM because this review was strictly read-only: the control flow and the skipped store are directly verifiable from the source and the documented finalize contract, but I did not build or run the extension to observe the resulting corruption. The same ordering defect appears in Database#close at database.c:107, where ctx->db is likewise nulled only on the non-raising path at database.c:109; I report it as downstream evidence under this one root control rather than as a separate finding.
findings.impact: SQLite3::Statement#close destroys the underlying sqlite3_stmt via sqlite3_finalize but leaves ctx->st pointing at the freed statement object whenever finalize reports a non-zero status, because rb_sqlite3_raise longjmps out of the function before ctx->st = NULL executes at statement.c:87. The Ruby object is left in a state that lies about itself: Statement#closed? returns false (statement.c:101 tests ctx->st) and REQUIRE_OPEN_STMT (statement.c:3-5) passes, so every subsequent method on that object passes the dangling pointer straight into libsqlite3. sqlite3_step, sqlite3_reset, sqlite3_bind_*, sqlite3_column_* and a second sqlite3_finalize are all reachable this way, and the SQLite documentation for sqlite3_finalize states that any use of a prepared statement after it has been finalized 'can result in undefined and undesirable behavior such as segfaults and heap corruption' (/usr/include/sqlite3.h:5306-5310). A second Statement#close reaches sqlite3_finalize on the freed pointer, which is a double free. In a long-lived process such as a Rails application, the freed sqlite3_stmt slab is likely to have been reused by other SQLite allocations, so the write side of a reused-memory bind or reset is a heap corruption primitive rather than only a crash.
evidence: ext/sqlite3/statement.c:85 - CHECK(db, sqlite3_finalize(ctx->st)) evaluates sqlite3_finalize as the macro argument, so the statement handle is destroyed and its memory released before the status is ever inspected.

ext/sqlite3/exception.h:4 - the CHECK macro expands to a bare rb_sqlite3_raise(_db, _status) call, so the destructive argument at statement.c:85 is fully evaluated first and control then enters the raise helper.

ext/sqlite3/exception.c:7 - rb_sqlite3_raise switches on status and returns only for the exact value SQLITE_OK (exception.c:8-9); every other value selects an exception class, including the default RuntimeError branch at exception.c:90.

ext/sqlite3/exception.c:93 - rb_raise(klass, "%s", sqlite3_errmsg(db)) performs a non-local longjmp out of rb_sqlite3_raise and therefore out of sqlite3_rb_close, abandoning the rest of the caller's body.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:87 - ctx->st = NULL is the only cleanup that invalidates the freed pointer, and it sits after the CHECK, so the longjmp skips it; rg confirms statement.c:18 and statement.c:87 are the only two assignments to ctx->st in the file, so nothing else ever clears it.

/usr/include/sqlite3.h:5290-5295 - sqlite3_finalize returns a non-OK error code when the most recent evaluation of the statement failed, which is the attacker-reachable trigger: the deferred error of the previous sqlite3_step is resurfaced by finalize.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:131-179 - Statement#step returns early for SQLITE_ROW and SQLITE_DONE and only routes other codes to CHECK, so a step that fails with a deferred error (for example SQLITE_CONSTRAINT or SQLITE_BUSY from concurrent access) leaves the statement in the failed state that finalize will later report.

lib/sqlite3/database.rb:86-90 - Database#prepare wraps the caller's block in begin/ensure and calls stmt.close in the ensure clause, so the failing close runs during exception unwinding of a normal execute; this is the ordinary code path, not an exotic one.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:101 - Statement#closed? reports Qtrue only when ctx->st is NULL, so after the skipped assignment the object claims to still be open; this is the guard an application would use and it is ineffective.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:3-5 - REQUIRE_OPEN_STMT raises only when ctx->st is NULL, so the guard used by step (statement.c:113), bind_param (statement.c:196), reset! (statement.c:280), column_count (statement.c:311), column_name (statement.c:324), column_decltype (statement.c:340), bind_parameter_count (statement.c:356) and database_name (statement.c:369) passes with the dangling pointer.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:127 - sqlite3_step(stmt) is reached with the freed handle after REQUIRE_OPEN_STMT passes, dereferencing released memory; the parallel sinks are sqlite3_reset at statement.c:282, sqlite3_bind_* at statement.c:231-258 and a second sqlite3_finalize at statement.c:85.
lib/sqlite3/statement.rb:140-144 - the Ruby-side must_be_open! check delegates to the same closed? predicate, so the Ruby layer adds no compensating guard.
ext/sqlite3/statement.c:9-13 - the statement's GC free function only xfrees the wrapper struct and never touches ctx->st, confirming no later cleanup notices or repairs the stale pointer.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:107 - the same root-cause ordering appears in Database#close, where CHECK(db, sqlite3_close(ctx->db)) runs the destructor as the macro argument and ctx->db is nulled only afterwards at database.c:109, so a non-OK close leaves REQUIRE_OPEN_DB (database.c:3-5) passing with a stale handle.
preconditions: Application code prepares and executes a statement whose final sqlite3_step leaves a deferred error, so that sqlite3_finalize at statement.c:85 returns a non-OK status.

The application catches or survives the exception raised out of Statement#close (for example the SQLite3::Exception propagating from Database#prepare's ensure block) rather than terminating the process.

The same Statement object is then used again, either explicitly or through a retained ResultSet (lib/sqlite3/resultset.rb:66 calls @stmt.step, lib/sqlite3/resultset.rb:104 calls @stmt.close), or Statement#close is called a second time.

For memory corruption rather than a bare crash, the freed sqlite3_stmt allocation must be reused by other SQLite or process allocations between the finalize and the reuse, which is the normal condition in a long-running process.
exploitScenarios: The attacker supplies input that drives a statement whose execution fails with an error SQLite reports lazily, for example a constraint violation on an INSERT or SQLITE_BUSY caused by a second connection holding an exclusive transaction, so the prepared statement ends in a failed state.
The application's normal prepare/execute wrapper unwinds, and Database#prepare's ensure block at lib/sqlite3/database.rb:89 calls stmt.close.
sqlite3_finalize runs at statement.c:85 and frees the sqlite3_stmt, then returns the deferred non-OK error code.

rb_sqlite3_raise maps the code to an exception class and rb_raise at exception.c:93 longjmps out of sqlite3_rb_close, so statement.c:87 never sets ctx->st to NULL and the wrapper keeps the freed pointer.
The application rescues the exception, as retry and error-reporting code around database calls routinely does, and the Statement object survives with closed? still reporting false.

The attacker triggers a code path that touches the same Statement again, or simply a second close during cleanup, so REQUIRE_OPEN_STMT passes and the freed pointer reaches sqlite3_step, sqlite3_reset, sqlite3_bind_* or a second sqlite3_finalize.

The attacker shapes the intervening SQLite allocations, for example through the size of subsequently bound values or queried rows, so the freed slab is reoccupied by attacker-influenced bytes before the use, turning the use-after-free and double free into a heap corruption primitive.
recommendations: Clear ctx->st before the status is checked: capture the finalize result into a local, set ctx->st = NULL, and only then call CHECK, so the handle can never be reachable after it is destroyed regardless of how the raise unwinds. Apply the same ordering to Database#close at ext/sqlite3/database.c:107, where ctx->db is likewise nulled only on the non-raising path at database.c:109.

Stop embedding side-effecting calls in the CHECK macro argument. Give CHECK a do/while(0) body with parenthesised arguments so it cannot silently absorb a destructive expression, and require callers to evaluate the sqlite3 call into a local first.

Add a regression test that forces close to fail, for example by stepping a statement into a constraint violation or a SQLITE_BUSY from a competing exclusive transaction, rescuing the exception raised by Statement#close, and then asserting Statement#closed? is true and that a further step/bind_param/close raises SQLite3::Exception instead of crashing.

findings.title: Database#busy_handler installs the contention callback with sqlite3_trace, so no busy handler is ever registered
findings.rationale: This is a genuine access-decision defect rather than a style note: the control that is supposed to arbitrate contended access to the database file is never installed, and the method reports success anyway. I verified by search over ext/sqlite3/*.c that sqlite3_busy_handler appears nowhere in the extension, so the connection's busy-handler slot stays permanently empty while the application believes its policy is active. The guard that should have caught this is ineffective for a concrete reason I checked against the header: CHECK at database.c:218 inspects the return of sqlite3_trace, which is the previous trace user-data pointer rather than an error code (/usr/include/sqlite3.h:3342-3343), so a successful-looking status is returned to Ruby at database.c:220 regardless. The mistake also creates a second, distinct consequence, because the callback is bound into a slot with a different signature: SQLite invokes the tracer as void(void*, const char *sql) while rb_sqlite3_busy_handler is int(void*, int) and immediately evaluates INT2NUM((long)count) at database.c:180, so a libsqlite3-owned SQL text pointer is reinterpreted as a count and surfaced to Ruby as an Integer on every statement. A third effect follows from the documented single-tracer rule at /usr/include/sqlite3.h:3415-3418: registering a busy handler silently uninstalls any tracer from Database#trace at database.c:171, and vice versa. I confirmed no Ruby-side shim compensates, since lib/sqlite3/database.rb:233 only aliases busy_timeout. Severity is MEDIUM because the harm is real but bounded, requiring either live lock contention or the application to surface the callback argument. Difficulty is LOW because creating contention needs nothing more than a second connection holding an exclusive transaction, which the repository's own tests already demonstrate. Confidence is MEDIUM because the missing registration is directly verifiable from source, but I did not execute anything, so the precise runtime outcome of the pointer-as-int mismatch is inferred from the two declarations rather than observed. The existing tests at test/test_integration_pending.rb:38 assert only that the handler is called, never that it governs contention or that its argument is a plausible retry count, which is why the defect survived.
findings.impact: Database#busy_handler registers the caller's contention-arbitration callback with sqlite3_trace instead of sqlite3_busy_handler, so no busy handler is ever installed on the connection. Two things follow. First, the application's lock-contention decision never runs: every callback that was supposed to decide whether to wait or abort is silently ignored, and contended operations fail immediately with SQLITE_BUSY, which the caller believes it had arranged to handle. Second, the callback is instead wired into the trace slot, whose callback SQLite invokes with (void*, const char *sql) while rb_sqlite3_busy_handler is declared as (void*, int) and immediately does INT2NUM((long)count) at database.c:180. On every statement executed on that connection, a libsqlite3-owned SQL text pointer is reinterpreted as an integer count and converted into a Ruby Fixnum handed to the application's callback, leaking heap address bits into Ruby-visible data. Because sqlite3_trace also documents that each call overrides all prior trace callbacks (/usr/include/sqlite3.h:3415-3418), calling busy_handler additionally uninstalls any tracer previously registered by Database#trace, and vice versa, so registering one silently disables the other.
evidence: ext/sqlite3/database.c:201 - busy_handler is the public SQLite3::Database#busy_handler method, bound at database.c:591, and is the documented way an application installs its lock-contention policy (see the call-seq comment at database.c:187-199).
ext/sqlite3/database.c:211 - the caller-supplied block or callable object is captured, and database.c:213 stores it in @busy_handler where the C callback later reads it.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:215-216 - the registration call is sqlite3_trace(ctx->db, ..., rb_sqlite3_busy_handler, (void *)self); rg over ext/sqlite3/*.c confirms sqlite3_busy_handler is never called anywhere in the extension, so the busy-handler slot on the connection stays empty.

/usr/include/sqlite3.h:2861 - the real registration API is sqlite3_busy_handler(sqlite3*, int(*)(void*,int), void*); it is a distinct slot from the tracer and is the only way to install the callback SQLite consults on lock contention.
/usr/include/sqlite3.h:3342-3343 - sqlite3_trace's callback type is void(*xTrace)(void*, const char*), so passing rb_sqlite3_busy_handler here binds an int-taking function into a pointer-taking slot.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:176-180 - rb_sqlite3_busy_handler is defined as int(void *ctx, int count) and evaluates INT2NUM((long)count); when SQLite invokes it as a tracer, count receives the const char * SQL pointer, so a heap address becomes the Ruby Integer passed to the application callback.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:218 - CHECK(ctx->db, status) inspects only the value returned by sqlite3_trace, which returns the previous trace user-data pointer rather than an error code, so the guard cannot detect that the wrong slot was written and the method returns self at database.c:220 as if registration succeeded.

/usr/include/sqlite3.h:3415-3418 - each sqlite3_trace call cancels all prior trace callbacks and a connection may have at most one, which is why this registration also silently removes any tracer installed by Database#trace at database.c:171.
lib/sqlite3/database.rb:233 - the Ruby layer only aliases busy_timeout to busy_timeout=; there is no Ruby-side busy_handler shim that could compensate, so the C behaviour is what applications get.

test/test_integration_pending.rb:38 - the busy-handler tests live in the file the introducing commit titled 'pending tests work' and assert the handler is called; nothing in the suite asserts that the handler actually governs lock contention or that its argument is a real retry count, so the mismatch is not caught by existing coverage.
preconditions: The application calls SQLite3::Database#busy_handler to install a contention policy, which is the documented API for that purpose (database.c:187-199).
For the availability half: two connections contend for the same database file so that SQLite would consult the busy handler, for example one holding an exclusive transaction while another writes.
For the address-leak half: at least one statement is executed on the connection after busy_handler is called, since the tracer fires per statement.

I did not execute the extension or the test suite in this read-only review, so the concrete crash-versus-garbage-value outcome of the (void*, const char*) versus (void*, int) mismatch is inferred from the two declarations rather than observed; the missing sqlite3_busy_handler registration is directly verifiable from the source.
exploitScenarios: The operator installs a busy handler intended to bound waiting and to abort on contention, and reasonably believes contention is now under application control because the method returned successfully.
The attacker opens a second connection to the same database file and holds an exclusive transaction, or simply issues concurrent writes, creating lock contention.
SQLite consults its busy-handler slot, finds it empty because database.c:215 wrote the tracer slot instead, and returns SQLITE_BUSY immediately without ever invoking the application's policy.

The application's contention policy never runs, so the failure mode the operator explicitly configured against occurs: writes fail immediately under contention with no retry and no bound on the caller's own error handling.

In parallel, each statement the attacker causes to execute makes SQLite invoke the tracer slot with a const char * SQL pointer, which rb_sqlite3_busy_handler converts at database.c:180 into a Ruby Integer and passes to the application callback.

The attacker reads that integer wherever the application logs or echoes its busy-handler argument, recovering heap address bits that defeat address-space layout randomisation for a follow-on memory attack.
Because sqlite3_trace permits only one callback, the same call also silently removes any tracer the application had installed for auditing, so statement-level audit logging stops without any error.
recommendations: Register the callback with sqlite3_busy_handler(ctx->db, rb_sqlite3_busy_handler, (void *)self) so the callback lands in the slot SQLite actually consults for lock contention, and keep sqlite3_trace exclusively for Database#trace's void(void*, const char*) tracefunc.

Make the two callback types impossible to confuse: keep the busy handler's int(void*, int) signature and the tracer's void(void*, const char*) signature distinct, and build with warnings that reject an incompatible function-pointer argument so this substitution fails to compile rather than being accepted silently.

Add a regression test that installs a busy handler, creates real contention from a second connection, and asserts both that the handler is invoked and that its argument is a small monotonically increasing retry count rather than a large pointer-like value; add a companion test asserting that installing a busy handler does not uninstall a previously registered tracer.

findings.title: Use-after-free and double free: SQLite3::Statement#close finalizes the statement before nulling the handle, so a failing close leaves a dangling sqlite3_stmt that all closed? guards report as open
findings.rationale: sqlite3_finalize() is evaluated as the CHECK macro argument, so the statement is deallocated before rb_sqlite3_raise decides whether to longjmp. Per /usr/include/sqlite3.h, finalize frees the statement unconditionally but returns the deferred error code of the most recent failed step, so any attacker-triggerable step failure (SQLITE_CONSTRAINT from submitted data, SQLITE_BUSY from a concurrent writer) makes CHECK raise after the free and skip 'ctx->st = NULL' on the next line. The struct field keeps a pointer to freed memory, and every open/closed predicate in the gem tests only '!ctx->st', so REQUIRE_OPEN_STMT, closed_p, ResultSet#closed? and Statement#must_be_open! all report the freed statement as open. The gem itself supplies the second close: Database#query has an unconditional 'ensure result.close' while its own documentation instructs callers to close the ResultSet too. The path is complete from untrusted SQL/bind data to a use-after-free read and a double sqlite3_finalize, with no effective defense at any hop. Confidence is HIGH because every hop is verified in source and against the installed SQLite header; exploitation beyond a crash was not executed, which is reflected in difficulty rather than confidence.
findings.impact: A failing SQLite3::Statement#close leaves ctx->st pointing at a sqlite3_stmt that libsqlite3 has already deallocated, while every closed? guard in the gem still reports the statement as open. Any later use of that statement object dereferences freed heap memory, and a second close calls sqlite3_finalize() on the freed pointer, which is a double free. sqlite3.h states that use of a finalized statement 'can result in undefined and undesirable behavior such as segfaults and heap corruption'. An attacker who can induce a step error on a statement the application still holds gets a remotely triggerable heap-corruption primitive in-process, and at minimum a reliable crash of the Ruby VM. Because the error is deferred and re-reported by finalize, the exact failure the attacker causes (a UNIQUE constraint violation from submitted data, or SQLITE_BUSY from a concurrent writer) is what arms the bug.
evidence: lib/sqlite3/database.rb:201 - Database#query is a public API that prepares and executes caller-supplied SQL with caller-supplied bind values; it is the untrusted entry point that reaches the vulnerable control.

lib/sqlite3/statement.rb:65 - Statement#execute stores '@results = ResultSet.new(@connection, self)', and lib/sqlite3/resultset.rb:36 stores '@stmt = stmt', so the Statement object outlives the query frame and stays reachable from caller code after any exception.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:127 - 'int value = sqlite3_step(stmt);' returns the engine result for the attacker-influenced operation; attacker data that violates a UNIQUE or NOT NULL column yields SQLITE_CONSTRAINT, and a concurrent writer yields SQLITE_BUSY. Because the statement was prepared with sqlite3_prepare_v2 (statement.c:53), the specific code is returned directly.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:178 - the step switch default branch 'CHECK(sqlite3_db_handle(ctx->st), value);' forwards that non-OK code, raising a Ruby exception out of Statement#step and beginning stack unwinding with the statement still open.

lib/sqlite3/database.rb:206 - the 'ensure' clause of Database#query runs during that unwinding and calls 'result.close' at line 207; lib/sqlite3/resultset.rb:104 delegates straight to '@stmt.close'. This is an unconditional close with no closed? guard.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:82 - 'REQUIRE_OPEN_STMT(ctx);' is the only guard on the close path, and its definition at statement.c:3-5 tests solely 'if(!_ctxt->st)'. It is checked and ineffective against a stale non-NULL pointer.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:85 - 'CHECK(db, sqlite3_finalize(ctx->st));' is the root control. sqlite3_finalize deallocates the statement unconditionally, yet /usr/include/sqlite3.h documents 'If the most recent evaluation of statement S failed, then sqlite3_finalize(S) returns the appropriate error code or extended error code', so the deferred SQLITE_CONSTRAINT or SQLITE_BUSY is returned here after the free has already happened.
ext/sqlite3/exception.h:4 - '#define CHECK(_db, _status) rb_sqlite3_raise(_db, _status);' calls the raiser unconditionally, with the freeing sqlite3_finalize() call evaluated as the macro argument.

ext/sqlite3/exception.c:8 - rb_sqlite3_raise returns early only for exact equality with SQLITE_OK; every other status falls through to exception.c:93 'rb_raise(klass, "%s", sqlite3_errmsg(db));', a non-local longjmp.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:87 - 'ctx->st = NULL;' sits after the CHECK and is therefore skipped by the longjmp. The struct field (ext/sqlite3/statement.h:7) retains a pointer to freed memory. This ordering is the root cause.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:101 - closed_p returns Qtrue only when 'if(!ctx->st)', so Statement#closed?, ResultSet#closed? (lib/sqlite3/resultset.rb:109) and Statement#must_be_open! (lib/sqlite3/statement.rb:141) all report the freed statement as still open. Every application-level guard is defeated.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:84 - on a second close, 'sqlite3 * db = sqlite3_db_handle(ctx->st);' reads the freed sqlite3_stmt allocation before statement.c:85 calls sqlite3_finalize on it again, producing the use-after-free read and the double free.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:9 - the GC free function 'deallocate' only performs 'xfree(c)' and never finalizes, and ext/sqlite3/database.c:16 sweeps via sqlite3_next_stmt which no longer lists the already-freed statement, so nothing reclaims or neutralizes the dangling pointer.

git blame ext/sqlite3/statement.c -L 84,87 - lines 84-85 are commit da74b8e ('centralizing exception handling, removing dead code') and line 87 is cd7ae9d ('statement closing works now'); the raise-before-null-out ordering has existed since the C rewrite and no commit has ever reordered it or added a null-out on the error path.
exploitScenarios: The victim application calls Database#query (lib/sqlite3/database.rb:201) with a block, or Database#prepare without a block (lib/sqlite3/database.rb:84), so a Statement or ResultSet reference survives the call.

The attacker supplies input that makes sqlite3_step return a non-OK code, for example a value that duplicates a UNIQUE column to force SQLITE_CONSTRAINT, or opens a concurrent write transaction to force SQLITE_BUSY.
statement.c:178 raises that code out of Statement#step, unwinding the stack while ctx->st is still set.
The unwinding runs the ensure clause at lib/sqlite3/database.rb:207, which calls close on the same statement.
REQUIRE_OPEN_STMT at statement.c:82 passes, and sqlite3_finalize at statement.c:85 frees the statement and returns the same deferred error code.
CHECK raises again via exception.c:93, so statement.c:87 never executes and ctx->st keeps the freed pointer while closed? still reports false.

The attacker triggers one more operation on the retained object, either a second close (the documented caller-side close at lib/sqlite3/database.rb:197-200 plus the library's own ensure gives exactly two closes) or any method such as step, bind_param, columns or types, all of which pass the ineffective REQUIRE_OPEN_STMT guard.

sqlite3_db_handle and sqlite3_finalize operate on freed heap memory, corrupting the SQLite/malloc heap or crashing the process; with repeated triggers the attacker grooms the freed chunk to control the memory that the second finalize writes through.
preconditions: The application retains a reference to a Statement or ResultSet past an operation that raised, which the gem's own Database#query ensure path and the no-block Database#prepare and Database#query return paths all produce.

The attacker can influence data or concurrency such that sqlite3_step returns a non-OK result code, for example SQLITE_CONSTRAINT from submitted data, SQLITE_BUSY from a concurrent writer, or SQLITE_CORRUPT/SQLITE_IOERR from a hostile or damaged database file.

The application catches or otherwise survives the first exception and reaches a second use or second close of the same statement object, which the documented close contract at lib/sqlite3/database.rb:197-200 actively encourages.
Turning the double free into anything beyond a crash additionally requires heap grooming of the libsqlite3 allocator, which needs product knowledge and favorable allocation timing.
recommendations: Root-cause fix: clear the handle before it can be reported as an error. In sqlite3_rb_close, capture the pointer, null out ctx->st first, then finalize and check, for example 'sqlite3_stmt *st = ctx->st; ctx->st = NULL; sqlite3 *db = sqlite3_db_handle(st); CHECK(db, sqlite3_finalize(st));' so the raise cannot leave a dangling pointer behind.
Apply the same ordering to the identical pattern in Database#close at ext/sqlite3/database.c:107, where 'CHECK(db, sqlite3_close(ctx->db));' precedes 'ctx->db = NULL;' at database.c:109.

Hardening: stop embedding side-effecting, resource-releasing calls in the CHECK macro argument (ext/sqlite3/exception.h:4), and parenthesize the macro arguments, so the release and the error check are visibly separate statements at every callsite.

Hardening: make the Statement GC free function at ext/sqlite3/statement.c:9-13 the single owner of finalization, and track a separate explicit 'closed' flag rather than overloading the raw pointer as the open/closed predicate used by closed_p (statement.c:101) and REQUIRE_OPEN_STMT (statement.c:3-5).

Regression test: prepare a statement against a table with a UNIQUE constraint, step it into SQLITE_CONSTRAINT so close raises, then assert that stmt.closed? is true and that a second stmt.close and a stmt.step both raise the ordinary 'cannot use a closed statement' error rather than touching freed memory. Run it under valgrind or ASAN so a regression surfaces as a use-after-free report instead of passing silently.

findings.title: Function-pointer type confusion: Database#busy_handler registers an int(void*,int) callback through sqlite3_trace, so no busy handler is installed and the block is invoked as a tracer on every statement
findings.snippet:
int status = sqlite3_trace(
      ctx->db, NIL_P(block) ? NULL : rb_sqlite3_busy_handler, (void *)self);
findings.rationale: The registration calls the wrong libsqlite3 API, installing a callback declared 'int (*)(void *, int)' into a slot whose declared type is 'void (*)(void *, const char *)'. sqlite3_busy_handler is never referenced anywhere in the extension, so the retry protection the application asked for is simply absent, and libsqlite3 instead calls the mismatched pointer as a tracer for every executed statement, reinterpreting a const char* SQL pointer as the integer count handed to user Ruby code. Calling through an incompatible function-pointer type is undefined behavior and is rejected outright under indirect-call CFI or Windows CFG. The CHECK on the next line cannot catch the mistake because sqlite3_trace returns the previous callback pointer rather than a status code. Severity is MEDIUM because the harm is bounded to a non-default API: applications that use only busy_timeout= are unaffected, and on mainstream x86-64 the mismatch degrades to argument truncation plus missing retry rather than memory corruption. Difficulty is LOW because forcing lock contention needs only a second connection.
findings.impact: Database#busy_handler registers its callback with sqlite3_trace() instead of sqlite3_busy_handler(), passing a function pointer of type 'int (*)(void *, int)' where libsqlite3 expects 'void (*)(void *, const char *)'. Two things follow. First, no busy handler is ever installed, so an application that explicitly asked for retry-on-contention silently gets none and fails with SQLITE_BUSY the moment any other writer holds the lock, which an attacker able to open a second connection can force at will. Second, libsqlite3 invokes the mismatched pointer as a trace callback on every statement, so the user's busy_handler block is called for every SQL statement with the low bits of the SQL text pointer reinterpreted as the integer 'count' argument. Calling a function through an incompatible function-pointer type is undefined behavior; on builds with indirect-call CFI or Windows Control Flow Guard it aborts the process, turning ordinary query execution into a denial of service. The call also clobbers any tracer installed by Database#trace, and busy_handler(nil) uninstalls that tracer rather than a busy handler.
evidence: lib/sqlite3/database.rb:36 - Pragmas is mixed into Database and busy_handler is exposed to Ruby at ext/sqlite3/database.c:591 via rb_define_method(cSqlite3Database, "busy_handler", busy_handler, -1), so this is a public, directly callable API.
ext/sqlite3/database.c:176 - 'static int rb_sqlite3_busy_handler(void * ctx, int count)' declares the callback with the busy-handler signature: it returns int and takes an int retry count.
ext/sqlite3/database.c:215 - the registration calls sqlite3_trace(), not sqlite3_busy_handler(); this is the root control where the wrong API is selected.
ext/sqlite3/database.c:216 - 'ctx->db, NIL_P(block) ? NULL : rb_sqlite3_busy_handler, (void *)self);' passes the int(void*,int) pointer as the xTrace argument.

/usr/include/sqlite3.h:3342 - the expected type is 'SQLITE_API SQLITE_DEPRECATED void *sqlite3_trace(sqlite3*, void(*xTrace)(void*,const char*), void*);', a void-returning callback whose second parameter is a const char* SQL string, which does not match the registered function.

/usr/include/sqlite3.h:2861 - the API the code intended, 'SQLITE_API int sqlite3_busy_handler(sqlite3*,int(*)(void*,int),void*);', has exactly the signature of rb_sqlite3_busy_handler and is never referenced anywhere in the extension.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:176 - grep across ext/ shows sqlite3_busy_handler appears only as this local function name and its use at database.c:216; the real libsqlite3 registration function is never called, confirming no busy handler is installed on any code path.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:180 - when libsqlite3 invokes the pointer as a tracer, 'rb_funcall(handle, rb_intern("call"), 1, INT2NUM((long)count));' converts the reinterpreted second argument, actually a const char* to the SQL text, into a Ruby Integer and passes it to the user block on every executed statement.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:171 - Database#trace registers the genuine tracer 'sqlite3_trace(ctx->db, NIL_P(block) ? NULL : tracefunc, (void *)self);' on the same slot, so the two features silently overwrite each other and busy_handler(nil) at database.c:216 passes NULL and removes the tracer.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:218 - 'CHECK(ctx->db, status);' checks the return of sqlite3_trace, which returns the previous callback pointer (void*) rather than a status code, so this check is meaningless and cannot detect the misregistration.

test/test_integration_pending.rb:22 - the only coverage, test_busy_handler_outwait and test_busy_handler_impatient at line 53, lives in the 'pending' test file and is therefore not exercised, which is why the misregistration has gone unnoticed.
git blame ext/sqlite3/database.c -L 215,218 - all four lines are commit 93ce604f (Aaron Patterson, 2010-01-24); the wrong API has been used since the feature was introduced.
exploitScenarios: The victim application calls db.busy_handler { |count| ... } expecting retry-on-contention, per the documented contract at ext/sqlite3/database.c:191-199.
database.c:215 registers the handler through sqlite3_trace, so libsqlite3's busy-handler slot stays empty and the pointer lands in the trace slot instead.
The attacker opens a second connection or process to the same database file and holds a write transaction open.

The victim's next conflicting statement immediately raises SQLite3::BusyException via the step path at ext/sqlite3/statement.c:178 with no retry, denying service to a request the application was written to survive.

Independently, on every statement the victim executes, libsqlite3 calls the mismatched pointer as a tracer, invoking the user's block with the truncated SQL-text pointer as 'count' and executing arbitrary application callback code on a hot path it was never meant to run on.

If the extension is built with clang -fsanitize=cfi-icall or on Windows with Control Flow Guard, the indirect call through the incompatible function-pointer type is rejected and the process aborts, so any attacker who can cause one SQL statement to execute crashes the service.
preconditions: The application calls Database#busy_handler; applications that use only Database#busy_timeout= (ext/sqlite3/database.c:535) are unaffected because that path calls the correct API.
For the availability impact, the attacker needs to create lock contention, for example a second connection or process writing to the same database file.

For the process-abort impact, the extension must be built with indirect-call control-flow integrity enforcement; on a mainstream x86-64 System V build the mismatch degrades to argument truncation and the missing handler rather than memory corruption.
recommendations: Root-cause fix: register the callback with the matching API, replacing the sqlite3_trace call at ext/sqlite3/database.c:215-216 with 'int status = sqlite3_busy_handler(ctx->db, NIL_P(block) ? NULL : rb_sqlite3_busy_handler, (void *)self);' so the function-pointer type matches the slot and a busy handler is actually installed.

Hardening: stop discarding the distinction between a status code and a returned pointer. sqlite3_trace returns the previous callback, so the CHECK at database.c:218 is checking a pointer as a status; assign each registration's result to a correctly typed variable so a future mismatch fails to compile.

Hardening: build the extension with -Wincompatible-pointer-types promoted to an error, and consider -fsanitize=cfi-icall in CI, so passing an int(void*,int) where void(void*,const char*) is expected is caught at compile time rather than at runtime.

Regression test: promote the busy-handler tests out of test/test_integration_pending.rb into the active suite. Hold a write lock from a second connection, assert that the block registered by db.busy_handler is actually invoked with a small monotonically increasing integer count, and assert that a block returning false produces SQLite3::BusyException while a block returning true retries. Add a separate assertion that db.busy_handler does not disturb a tracer installed by db.trace.

context_updates.response.researcher:
## Outcome

**No panel-verifiable findings in this component under the crypto-and-secrets lens.** The error-translation path contains no cryptography, no randomness, no key or nonce material, and no credential handling, so the lens has no live surface to land on here.

**What I read in full:** `ext/sqlite3/exception.c` (all 94 lines), `ext/sqlite3/exception.h` (all 8 lines), plus every one of the 12 `CHECK` callsites in `ext/sqlite3/database.c` and `ext/sqlite3/statement.c`, `lib/sqlite3/errors.rb`, `lib/sqlite3/database.rb`, `ext/sqlite3/sqlite3_ruby.h`, `ext/sqlite3/sqlite3.c`, and `ext/sqlite3/extconf.rb`.

**Hypotheses I tried to close and why each failed:**

- **Secret disclosure through the raise sink.** `exception.c:93` copies a libsqlite3 message (SQL fragments, paths, schema identifiers) into a Ruby exception. But the message is delivered synchronously to the same in-process caller who supplied that SQL and that path, so it discloses nothing the caller does not already hold. There is no cross-tenant hop: every callsite passes its own connection, either `ctx->db` or `sqlite3_db_handle(ctx->st)`. Whether an application later renders the message to an end user is the application's decision, not a library defect.
- **Credential material in the error text.** There is no SQLCipher or encryption support to leak a key through. A repository-wide search of all 72 tracked files for `rekey`, `hexkey`, `PRAGMA key`, `cipher`, and `crypt` returned nothing outside unrelated `primary key` DDL in tests.
- **Hardcoded secrets.** No private-key blocks, AWS/Slack/GitHub/Stripe tokens, or JWTs in any tracked file.
- **Weak crypto, weak randomness, key/nonce reuse.** The component and the whole extension make no crypto or RNG calls; `sqlite3.c:21` calls only `sqlite3_initialize()`.
- **Timing side channel.** `exception.c:7` switches on an `int` result code. No secret-dependent comparison exists in the component or the repository.
- **Prompt injection.** No agent-instruction files exist, and a search of tracked non-harness files for steering phrases found none.

**Two things worth recording as verified non-issues,** because the supplied threat model flags them as suspicious and a future reviewer will re-raise them. Neither is a vulnerability:

- `statement.c:85` — `CHECK(db, sqlite3_finalize(ctx->st))` is not a use-after-free. `sqlite3_finalize` destroys the statement, not the connection, and `db` is captured at `statement.c:84` before the call, so the handle `exception.c:93` dereferences is still live.
- `database.c:107` — `CHECK(db, sqlite3_close(ctx->db))` is not a use-after-free either. On `SQLITE_OK` the raise function returns at `exception.c:9` without touching `db`; on the failure path (`SQLITE_BUSY` from unfinalized statements) `sqlite3_close` leaves the handle allocated.

**Not verified:** I did not execute anything, per the read-only rule. My reading of `sqlite3_errmsg(NULL)` as null-safe rests on upstream SQLite behavior rather than source in this tree — the repository links system libsqlite3 and vendors no amalgamation (`tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:35` downloads it at build time). That gap does not affect the empty result, since `database.c:80` is the only callsite that could pass a null handle and it falls under the memory lens rather than this one.

findings.title: Custom SQL function block is handed to SQLite as unrooted user data, allowing use-after-free on invocation
findings.rationale: The Ruby Proc registered as a SQL user-defined function is passed to sqlite3_create_function as opaque pApp user data and is never rooted: define_function performs no rb_iv_set, the project contains zero occurrences of rb_gc_mark, rb_gc_register_address or rb_global_variable, both Data_Wrap_Struct calls pass a NULL mark function, the wrapped structs contain no VALUE slots, and the Ruby caller at lib/sqlite3/database.rb:259 creates the wrapper Proc inline without storing it. The trampoline later resurrects the raw word via sqlite3_user_data and dispatches a method on it. The same file uses the safe pattern (store callable in an ivar, pass self as user data) for trace, busy_handler and authorizer, which shows this is an omission rather than a deliberate contract, so the path from a normal API call to a use-after-free is complete and unguarded.
findings.impact: The Ruby Proc implementing a user-defined SQL function is reachable only through a raw machine word stored inside SQLite's function table, which the Ruby garbage collector never scans. After any GC cycle the object slot can be freed and reused, yet the next SQL statement that calls the function dispatches `call` on that stale VALUE. This is a use-after-free that degenerates into type confusion when the slot has been recycled into an attacker-influenced object: the process can crash, invoke an unintended method on an unrelated object, or, with heap grooming, be steered toward controlled execution inside the application process. Every application using Database#create_function or #define_function is affected, and the same weakness exists in weaker form for aggregates, where only the most recently registered aggregator is retained.
evidence: lib/sqlite3/database.rb:258 - Database#create_function is the public, documented API an application calls to register a Ruby callback for use inside SQL; it is the entry point for this control.

lib/sqlite3/database.rb:259 - `define_function(name) do |*args| ... end` builds a brand-new wrapper Proc inline and passes it as a block; this Proc is never assigned to a local, an instance variable, or any collection, so after the call returns the only surviving reference is whatever the C layer keeps.
ext/sqlite3/database.c:319 - `VALUE block = rb_block_proc();` captures that Proc into a plain C automatic variable inside define_function, which stops being a GC root as soon as the function returns.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:326 - the Proc is cast to `(void *)` and passed as the pApp user-data argument of sqlite3_create_function, so SQLite stores it as an opaque machine word in its own function table; this is the handoff that loses GC visibility.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:313-335 - the whole body of define_function was read: it contains no rb_iv_set, no rb_gc_register_address, no rb_global_variable, and no Ruby-side container write. The rooting guard one would expect here is simply absent, not merely weak.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:321-330 - the 8-argument sqlite3_create_function is used rather than sqlite3_create_function_v2, so there is also no xDestroy hook that could manage the reference lifetime; a repository-wide search for sqlite3_create_function_v2 and xDestroy returns nothing.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:27 - the Database object is wrapped with `Data_Wrap_Struct(klass, NULL, deallocate, ctx)`; the mark-function argument is NULL, so the wrapper itself cannot mark any child VALUE. The equivalent Statement allocator at ext/sqlite3/statement.c:21 is also NULL-marked.
ext/sqlite3/database.h:6-8 - `struct _sqlite3Ruby` contains only `sqlite3 *db`, so there is no VALUE slot a mark function could ever have reported even if one existed.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:169, ext/sqlite3/database.c:213, ext/sqlite3/database.c:514 - by contrast the trace, busy_handler and authorizer callbacks each store their callable in an instance variable and pass `(void *)self` as user data, re-fetching the callable at invocation time. This proves the safe pattern was known in this same file and was not applied to define_function.
ext/sqlite3/database.c:288 - when SQL later invokes the function, the trampoline recovers the raw word with `VALUE callable = (VALUE)sqlite3_user_data(ctx);`, with no validity check of any kind.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:295 - `rb_funcall2(callable, rb_intern("call"), argc, params);` performs method dispatch on that VALUE. If a collection has occurred since registration, this reads an object header out of a freed or recycled slot: the dangerous operation completing the path.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:390 - the aggregate registration path does `rb_iv_set(self, "@agregator", aggregator)`, but this is a single slot with no reader and no array, so registering a second aggregator on the same Database silently unroots the first while SQLite at ext/sqlite3/database.c:384 still holds its raw pointer.
exploitScenarios: An application registers one or more SQL helper functions at startup, for example `db.create_function('normalize', 1) { |func, v| func.result = v.to_s.downcase }`, following the documented example at lib/sqlite3/database.rb:249-257.

create_function returns; the wrapper Proc created at lib/sqlite3/database.rb:259 now has zero references visible to the Ruby GC, because ext/sqlite3/database.c:326 stored it only as an opaque pointer inside SQLite.

The application continues serving traffic. Ordinary request handling allocates Ruby objects and triggers a garbage collection cycle, which reclaims the unreferenced Proc and returns its slot to the free list.

The attacker drives request traffic whose object allocation profile causes the freed slot to be reoccupied by an object whose contents the attacker influences, such as a String or Hash built from request parameters. This is the heap-grooming step that makes the outcome controlled rather than merely a crash.
The attacker issues a request that runs any query calling the registered function, for example a search endpoint whose SQL contains `normalize(name)`.

SQLite invokes ext/sqlite3/database.c:288, which resurrects the stale VALUE, and ext/sqlite3/database.c:295 dispatches `call` on the recycled slot, producing a use-after-free and type confusion in the application process.
preconditions: The application registers at least one custom SQL function through Database#create_function or Database#define_function, or more than one aggregate through create_aggregate / create_aggregate_handler.
A Ruby garbage collection cycle runs between registration and invocation, which is the normal steady state of any long-running process.
Some SQL executed afterwards invokes the registered function, which is the entire purpose of registering it.

For a controlled outcome rather than an unpredictable crash, the attacker must be able to influence Ruby heap allocation in the same process, for example by sending requests that allocate attacker-derived strings.
recommendations: Root cause: stop relying on SQLite to hold the only reference to a Ruby object. Keep a strong Ruby-side reference for the lifetime of the registration, for example an `@functions` Hash on the Database keyed by function name that is written in define_function before sqlite3_create_function is called, so the callable is reachable from a marked object.

Alternatively adopt the pattern already used by trace, busy_handler and authorizer: pass `(void *)self` as the user data and look the callable up from an instance variable inside rb_sqlite3_func at invocation time, which removes the raw-VALUE-as-pointer construct entirely.

Fix the aggregate path at ext/sqlite3/database.c:390 in the same change: `@agregator` is a single overwritable slot (and is misspelled), so replace it with a keyed collection that retains every registered aggregator.

If the raw user-data design is kept for compatibility, migrate to sqlite3_create_function_v2 with an xDestroy callback and pair it with rb_gc_register_address / rb_gc_unregister_address so the reference is explicitly rooted and released.
Give both Data_Wrap_Struct calls (ext/sqlite3/database.c:27 and ext/sqlite3/statement.c:21) a real mark function once the structs carry VALUE members, instead of NULL.

Regression test: register a custom function, discard all Ruby references to the block, call `GC.start` several times (and `GC.stress = true` in a dedicated test), then execute SQL invoking the function and assert the correct result rather than a crash or NoMethodError. Add the same test registering two different aggregators and exercising the first one after GC.

findings.title: UDF argument array is allocated with xcalloc, hiding live Ruby objects from the GC during conversion
findings.rationale: Newly allocated Ruby objects for each SQL function argument are written into malloc'd memory that Ruby's GC does not scan, while subsequent loop iterations keep allocating (rb_float_new, rb_tainted_str_new2) and can trigger a collection. No RB_GC_GUARD, temporary Array, or registration protects the block, and the whole unprotected array is then passed as the Ruby argument list. Attacker-controlled argument sizes and counts make the GC timing influenceable. Confidence is MEDIUM because conservative stack and register scanning may incidentally keep some values alive depending on compiler codegen, and settling that would require execution, which was not performed.
findings.impact: Newly created Ruby objects representing SQL function arguments are stored only in malloc'd memory, which Ruby's garbage collector does not scan. Converting later arguments allocates more Ruby objects and can trigger a collection that reclaims the already-converted earlier arguments. The freed VALUEs are then passed as the argument list to the application's Ruby callback, so user code operates on dangling or recycled objects. Because the attacker supplies the argument values and therefore controls both the number and size of the allocations, the GC timing is influenceable, making this the more deterministically reachable of the two use-after-free conditions in this trampoline.
evidence: lib/sqlite3/database.rb:258 - Database#create_function registers the Ruby callback that this trampoline ultimately invokes, and the SQL author controls the call site, the argument count and the argument values.
ext/sqlite3/database.c:286 - rb_sqlite3_func is the SQLite-side entry point, receiving argc and the sqlite3_value argument vector for each row the function is applied to.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:289 - the converted Ruby values are stored in `xcalloc`'d memory. Ruby's GC conservatively scans the machine stack and registers but does not scan arbitrary malloc'd heap blocks, so every VALUE written here is invisible to the collector.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:291-293 - the conversion loop assigns `params[i] = sqlite3val2rb(argv[i]);` one element at a time, so earlier elements sit unprotected in that block while later elements are still being produced.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:244 and ext/sqlite3/database.c:247 and ext/sqlite3/database.c:250 - sqlite3val2rb allocates fresh Ruby objects via rb_float_new and rb_tainted_str_new2 on each iteration; these are exactly the allocation points that can trigger a GC cycle in the middle of the loop.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:289-295 - the region was read in full: there is no rb_gc_register_address, no RB_GC_GUARD, no temporary Ruby Array, and no other rooting construct protecting params. A repository-wide search for rb_gc_mark, rb_gc_register_address and rb_global_variable returns zero occurrences anywhere in ext/, so the guard is absent project-wide.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:295 - `rb_funcall2(callable, rb_intern("call"), argc, params);` passes the entire unprotected array as the Ruby argument list, delivering any collected element to application code as a dangling VALUE: the dangerous operation.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:348-353 - rb_sqlite3_step repeats the identical xcalloc-then-convert-then-rb_funcall2 pattern for aggregate step callbacks, so the same defect is reachable through create_aggregate and create_aggregate_handler.
exploitScenarios: The application registers a multi-argument custom SQL function, for example `db.create_function('cmp', 3) { |func, a, b, c| ... }`, and exposes a query path that applies it to stored column data.

The attacker stores large text or blob values in the columns that will be passed to the function, so that each per-argument conversion at ext/sqlite3/database.c:247 or :250 allocates a substantial Ruby String.
The attacker triggers a query that applies the function across many rows, for example a report or search query, maximising allocation pressure inside the conversion loop.

During one invocation, the allocation for a later argument at ext/sqlite3/database.c:292 triggers a garbage collection. The already-converted earlier arguments live only in the xcalloc'd block at ext/sqlite3/database.c:289, are therefore unreachable, and are reclaimed.
The loop finishes and ext/sqlite3/database.c:295 passes the array, including the reclaimed slots, to the Ruby callback, which now reads and operates on freed or recycled objects.
preconditions: The application registers a custom function or aggregate whose callback takes at least two arguments, so that at least one conversion happens after another value is already stored in the array.
The attacker can influence the values passed to that function, typically by controlling data stored in the queried columns or the expressions in the query.
A garbage collection cycle occurs during the conversion loop; allocation pressure from large attacker-supplied values makes this reachable rather than incidental.

Confidence is MEDIUM rather than HIGH because Ruby's conservative stack and register scanning may incidentally keep some of these values alive depending on compiler register allocation; settling that would require execution, which I did not perform.
recommendations: Root cause: keep the converted arguments in GC-visible storage. Build the argument list in a Ruby Array created with rb_ary_new2 and populated with rb_ary_push, then dispatch with rb_apply or rb_funcall2 over RARRAY_PTR of that live array, so every element is marked for the whole lifetime of the call.

If a C array must be used, allocate it with ALLOCA_N so it lives on the machine stack that Ruby's conservative collector scans, or wrap it with rb_gc_register_address / rb_gc_unregister_address around the conversion and dispatch.
Apply the identical fix to rb_sqlite3_step at ext/sqlite3/database.c:345-355, which duplicates the pattern for aggregates.

Regression test: define a custom function taking several arguments, invoke it under `GC.stress = true` (or with an explicit GC.start forced from inside a preceding argument's conversion) against rows containing multi-megabyte strings, and assert that the callback receives the exact expected argument values rather than corrupted objects or a crash.

findings.title: busy_handler is registered through sqlite3_trace with an incompatible callback signature, leaking pointer bits into Ruby and never installing the handler
findings.rationale: Database#busy_handler passes an int(*)(void*,int) function pointer to sqlite3_trace, whose callback type is void(*)(void*,const char*). SQLite therefore invokes the handler for every statement, passing the SQL text pointer where the callee reads an int, and that pointer-derived value is boxed with INT2NUM and handed to the application's Ruby block. The real sqlite3_busy_handler API is never called anywhere in ext/, so the documented retry protection does not exist, and because trace and busy_handler share one slot, registering a busy handler silently disables an installed tracer. The CHECK at line 218 does not catch this because sqlite3_trace itself succeeds. All of this is directly readable in the code, hence HIGH confidence.
findings.impact: Database#busy_handler installs its callback into SQLite's trace slot instead of its busy-handler slot, and does so through a function pointer of an incompatible type. Three concrete consequences follow. First, SQLite invokes the handler for every executed statement with a `const char *` SQL pointer where the C function declares an `int count`, so the application's Ruby block receives the low 32 bits of a live heap address; any application that logs, returns, or otherwise surfaces that count discloses pointer bits and undermines ASLR for a follow-on memory attack. Second, no busy handler is ever installed, so the documented contention-retry protection silently does not exist and concurrent access raises BusyException instead. Third, because trace and busy_handler share the single sqlite3_trace slot, registering a busy handler silently disables an already-installed tracer, killing SQL audit logging without any error.
evidence: ext/sqlite3/database.c:591 - `rb_define_method(cSqlite3Database, "busy_handler", busy_handler, -1);` exposes this as a public method on SQLite3::Database, the same class the in-scope Ruby layer defines at lib/sqlite3/database.rb:35, so it is part of the component's public database API.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:201 - busy_handler(argc, argv, self) is the registration entry point an application calls, per the documented usage in the comment at ext/sqlite3/database.c:187-200 and exercised at test/test_integration_pending.rb:38.
ext/sqlite3/database.c:213 - the supplied block is stored in the @busy_handler instance variable, which is the reference the callback later reads.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:215-216 - the registration call is `sqlite3_trace(ctx->db, ... rb_sqlite3_busy_handler, (void *)self)`. sqlite3_trace's callback type is `void(*)(void*, const char*)`, but rb_sqlite3_busy_handler is `int(*)(void*, int)`. This is the incompatible-type handoff at the heart of the defect; it is a constraint violation that compilers only warn about, and ext/sqlite3/extconf.rb sets -Wall without -Werror, so the build proceeds.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:176 - `static int rb_sqlite3_busy_handler(void * ctx, int count)` declares the second parameter as int, so when SQLite passes the SQL text pointer in the second argument register the function reads the truncated low bits of that pointer as `count`.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:179-180 - `VALUE result = rb_funcall(handle, rb_intern("call"), 1, INT2NUM((long)count));` boxes that pointer-derived value and hands it directly to the application's Ruby block, which is the trust boundary where the leaked address bits become application-visible data.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:171 - trace() writes to the same single sqlite3_trace slot, so busy_handler and trace overwrite one another; whichever is called last wins and the other's callback is silently never invoked, while its instance variable still suggests it is active.

ext/sqlite3/database.c - a search of the entire ext/ tree for sqlite3_busy_handler finds only the local function name at line 176 and its use at line 216; the real SQLite sqlite3_busy_handler API is never called, confirming the retry protection is never installed. The guard one might expect, a CHECK of the registration result at ext/sqlite3/database.c:218, passes because sqlite3_trace itself succeeds.

test/test_integration_pending.rb:22-82 - the two tests that would have caught this live in the 'pending' test file, which explains why the defect survived; they are evidence about coverage, not part of the attack path.
exploitScenarios: An application registers a busy handler to survive database contention, for example `db.busy_handler { |count| sleep 0.01; count < 50 }`, exactly as documented at ext/sqlite3/database.c:187-199.
Because ext/sqlite3/database.c:216 wires the function into the trace slot, SQLite now calls it once for every statement executed rather than only on contention.
The attacker sends any ordinary request that causes a query to run, which is sufficient to invoke the callback.

SQLite passes the address of the SQL text buffer as the second argument; ext/sqlite3/database.c:176 reinterprets it as an int, and ext/sqlite3/database.c:180 delivers the low 32 bits of that live heap address to the application's block.

The attacker reads the leaked value wherever the application surfaces the retry count, such as a log line, an error message, a metrics label, or an admin page, and recovers heap address bits that defeat ASLR.

Separately, the attacker opens a concurrent connection and holds an exclusive transaction; because no real busy handler was ever installed, the victim's request fails with BusyException instead of retrying, turning ordinary contention into a denial of service, and any SQL tracer the application had installed for auditing has been silently disabled.
preconditions: The application calls Database#busy_handler, which is the documented way to configure contention behaviour.
For the pointer disclosure, the application must surface the block's count argument somewhere an attacker can observe, such as logs, an error response, or telemetry.

For the denial-of-service and lost-audit effects, no additional condition is required beyond calling busy_handler, since the handler is never installed and any existing tracer is overwritten unconditionally.
recommendations: Root cause: call the correct API. Replace sqlite3_trace at ext/sqlite3/database.c:215-216 with `sqlite3_busy_handler(ctx->db, NIL_P(block) ? NULL : rb_sqlite3_busy_handler, (void *)self)`, whose `int(*)(void*, int)` callback type matches rb_sqlite3_busy_handler exactly and gives `count` its intended meaning.

Hardening: build the extension with -Werror=incompatible-pointer-types (ext/sqlite3/extconf.rb already sets -Wall but not -Werror), so a mismatched callback type fails the build instead of producing a silent miscall.
Hardening: since trace and busy_handler are genuinely distinct SQLite slots once the correct API is used, add an assertion or test that installing one does not disable the other.

Regression test: promote the existing test/test_integration_pending.rb:22 and :53 busy-handler tests into the running suite so the handler's invocation and its `count` argument are asserted, and add a test that installs a tracer, then a busy handler, and asserts the tracer still receives executed SQL.

findings.title: Blob arguments to custom SQL functions are converted with a strlen-based constructor, over-reading past the blob and truncating at NUL
findings.rationale: The SQLITE_BLOB branch of the UDF argument converter builds a Ruby String with rb_tainted_str_new2, which derives length via strlen, and never calls sqlite3_value_bytes. SQLite guarantees NUL termination only for text results, not blobs, so the copy can run past the buffer into adjacent heap memory that is then delivered to application code. The correct length-bearing pattern is used in the row path at ext/sqlite3/statement.c:157-159, proving the omission. Confidence is MEDIUM because whether a given SQLite build leaves a particular blob unterminated depends on runtime allocator behaviour and would require execution to confirm; the embedded-NUL truncation effect, which can defeat validation functions, holds unconditionally.
findings.impact: Blob values passed as arguments to a Ruby-defined SQL function are converted into Ruby Strings by a constructor that derives the length with strlen, ignoring the length SQLite reports through sqlite3_value_bytes. SQLite guarantees NUL termination only for text results, not for blobs, so this walks past the end of the blob buffer until it happens to find a zero byte, copying adjacent process heap memory into a Ruby String that is then handed to application code. That is an out-of-bounds read yielding heap memory disclosure, and it can fault when the blob sits at the end of a mapped page. Independently and with certainty, any blob containing an embedded NUL is silently truncated at that byte, so a custom function used for validation, filtering, hashing or signature checking sees only a prefix of the real value and can be induced to approve data it never fully examined.
evidence: lib/sqlite3/database.rb:258 - Database#create_function is the public API that registers the Ruby callback; the SQL author decides which column values are passed to it, so any blob reachable by a query can become an argument.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:292 - rb_sqlite3_func converts every SQL argument through `params[i] = sqlite3val2rb(argv[i]);` before the Ruby callback is entered, making this the sole conversion path for UDF arguments.
ext/sqlite3/database.c:239 - sqlite3val2rb dispatches on `sqlite3_value_type(val)`, so a column or expression whose value is a blob takes the SQLITE_BLOB branch.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:250 - the SQLITE_BLOB branch calls rb_tainted_str_new2 on the pointer returned by sqlite3_value_blob. rb_tainted_str_new2 is the NUL-terminated-C-string constructor: it computes the length itself with strlen. No call to sqlite3_value_bytes appears anywhere in this function, or anywhere in ext/, so the authoritative length SQLite offers is never consulted. This is the dangerous operation.

ext/sqlite3/statement.c:157-159 - the ordinary row-reading path does the same conversion correctly: `rb_tainted_str_new(sqlite3_column_blob(stmt, i), sqlite3_column_bytes(stmt, i))` passes an explicit length. The same author used the length-bearing API here, which shows it was available and that ext/sqlite3/database.c:250 is an omission rather than a deliberate contract.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:247 - the adjacent SQLITE_TEXT branch uses the identical strlen-based constructor. SQLite does contractually NUL-terminate text, so that branch does not over-read, but it still truncates any text value containing an embedded NUL; documenting the contrast confirms the blob branch is the memory-safety one.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:295 - the resulting Ruby String is passed straight to the application callback as a function argument, so whatever bytes were copied past the end of the blob become ordinary application-visible data that can be returned to a caller, logged, or stored.

lib/sqlite3/statement.rb:4-8 - the library installs String#to_blob on every String in the process, and ext/sqlite3/statement.c:230-237 binds SQLite3::Blob values with sqlite3_bind_blob, giving an application a routine, documented way to place arbitrary attacker-supplied byte sequences, including ones with no NUL and ones with embedded NULs, into blob columns.
exploitScenarios: The application registers a custom SQL function that inspects stored binary data, for example `db.create_function('valid_sig', 1) { |func, data| func.result = check(data) ? 1 : 0 }`.

The attacker supplies binary content that the application stores in a blob column, using the ordinary upload or write path; SQLite3::Blob / String#to_blob at lib/sqlite3/statement.rb:5 is how the gem writes such values.
For the disclosure variant, the attacker crafts the blob so it contains no NUL byte, maximising how far strlen at ext/sqlite3/database.c:250 must scan beyond the end of the buffer.
The attacker triggers a query that applies the function to that row, for example a verification or search endpoint whose SQL calls `valid_sig(payload)`.

ext/sqlite3/database.c:250 constructs the Ruby String by scanning past the blob's real end, appending adjacent heap bytes, and ext/sqlite3/database.c:295 delivers that oversized String to the callback; whatever the application does with the value, such as echoing a normalised form or recording it, exposes the leaked memory.

For the truncation variant, the attacker instead places a NUL early in the blob so the callback only ever sees the harmless prefix, while the full attacker-controlled remainder stays in the database and is used later by code that reads the row through the correct length-aware path at ext/sqlite3/statement.c:157.
preconditions: The application registers at least one custom SQL function or aggregate through create_function, define_function, create_aggregate or create_aggregate_handler.
A blob-typed value reaches that function as an argument, which requires the attacker to influence stored binary data or the query expression.

For the out-of-bounds read specifically, SQLite must return a blob buffer that is not incidentally NUL-terminated. The documented API contract guarantees termination only for text, so the over-read is permitted by contract, but SQLite's internal allocator does terminate blobs on some code paths; confirming which paths over-read in a given build would require execution, which I did not perform, so confidence is MEDIUM. The embedded-NUL truncation effect holds unconditionally.
For the truncation to be a security bypass rather than a correctness bug, the custom function must be used for a validation, filtering or integrity decision.
recommendations: Root cause: use the length-bearing constructor. Replace ext/sqlite3/database.c:250 with `rb_tainted_str_new((const char *)sqlite3_value_blob(val), sqlite3_value_bytes(val))`, calling sqlite3_value_blob first and sqlite3_value_bytes second as the SQLite API requires, which matches the already-correct pattern at ext/sqlite3/statement.c:157-159.

Apply the same change to the SQLITE_TEXT branch at ext/sqlite3/database.c:247 so text values containing embedded NUL bytes are no longer silently truncated, and associate the database encoding with the resulting string as the statement path does at ext/sqlite3/statement.c:150.

Hardening: mark the blob result as an SQLite3::Blob rather than a plain String so callbacks can distinguish binary data from text, consistent with how the bind path treats blobs at ext/sqlite3/statement.c:230.

Regression test: register a custom function, store a blob containing an embedded NUL and a second blob with no NUL at all, invoke the function on both, and assert that the callback receives byte strings whose bytesize exactly equals the length originally written.
