output.researcher.rationale: I read tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake, tasks/native.rake, tasks/faq.rake, Rakefile, and setup.rb in full, plus the downstream boundary files the vendored artifacts reach (ext/sqlite3/extconf.rb, ext/sqlite3/sqlite3_ruby.h), and inspected 260 commits of history with the read-only git wrapper. I did not build, execute, install, fetch, or modify anything. Under the cryptography-and-secrets lens I ruled out most of the candidate surface with evidence: there are no hardcoded secrets or credentials in the working tree or in history (greps for password/secret/api-key/token/credential/PRIVATE KEY, plus git log --all -S'password' across all commits, return nothing but rubyforge URLs in docs); there is no use of rand, srand, Random, Digest, or OpenSSL anywhere in the component, so there is no weak-randomness, key/nonce-reuse, or timing-side-channel surface to report; and the .config file setup.rb persists (setup.rb:289-295, re-read at setup.rb:279-287) holds only program names and install paths, not credentials, so it is not a credential-exposure sink. The File.chmod 0777 at setup.rb:401 is an unsafe-looking API, but install destinations are root-owned and created via mkdir_p under the process umask, and I found no unprivileged path to pre-place a symlink there, so I did not report it. I also grepped repository content for agent-steering text (ignore-previous-instructions, do-not-report, already-audited claims) and found none, so there is no prompt-injection finding. The one genuine crypto-lens issue is the complete absence of transport authentication and artifact integrity verification on the vendored SQLite3 download chain: tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:36 and :46 pin a plaintext http:// scheme, lines 39 and 49 fetch with the result of system discarded, and no checksum, signature, or digest exists anywhere in the tree or in any of the 260 commits, so the bytes are unauthenticated when they become headers and an import library that ext/sqlite3/sqlite3_ruby.h:21 compiles into the published native extension. One bound I verified rather than assumed: the Rakefile at HEAD no longer imports tasks/*.rake (the loader was removed in commit fb1c2b1, which is an ancestor of HEAD) and there is no rakelib/ directory, so vendor:sqlite3 is not wired into the default build at HEAD even though the file is still shipped via Manifest.txt:32 and loads standalone. That reachability limit is recorded in the preconditions and is why confidence is MEDIUM; settling it definitively would require executing rake, which I did not do.

findings.title: Vendored SQLite3 build artifacts are fetched over plaintext HTTP with no checksum or signature verification, then compiled into the shipped native extension
findings.rationale: The vendoring chain has no transport authentication and no artifact integrity check of any kind: the scheme is hardcoded to plaintext http:// at tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:36 and :46, the fetch result is discarded at :39 and :49, and greps across the working tree and all 260 commits find no pinned digest, checksum, or signature. That makes the downloaded bytes fully attacker-controlled under an active network position, and those bytes cross into the compiler as sqlite3.h (ext/sqlite3/sqlite3_ruby.h:21) and into the linker as the generated import library, so a missing-cryptographic-verification weakness becomes build-host code execution and a supply-chain compromise of the published gem. The only checks on the path, find_header and find_library at ext/sqlite3/extconf.rb:19-20, test for a file name and one symbol and therefore do not establish authenticity.
findings.impact: An attacker with an active network position between the build host and www.sqlite.org (hostile Wi-Fi or proxy, ARP/DNS spoofing, BGP hijack, or a compromised CDN/mirror node) fully controls the bytes of both vendored archives, because the transfer has no TLS and there is no checksum, signature, or size check anywhere before the bytes are used. The substituted amalgamation zip supplies vendor/sqlite3/include/sqlite3.h, which ext/sqlite3/sqlite3_ruby.h:21 #includes into every translation unit of the extension, so attacker-authored C text is compiled into the loadable object. The substituted sqlitedll zip supplies the DLL from which the import library is generated and linked. This yields code execution in the build/cross-compile environment and, because the resulting object is packaged and published, a supply-chain compromise of the gem that lands in every consuming Ruby process. Separately, because extraction runs an external unzip with no member filtering, a hostile archive can also write files outside vendor/ on the build host.
evidence: tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:36 — builds the download URL with a hardcoded `http://` scheme (`url = "http://www.sqlite.org/#{File.basename(t.name)}"`); no TLS means the response body is not authenticated in any way and is fully attacker-controlled under an active network position.

tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:39 — the dangerous operation: `system "wget -c #{url} || curl -C - -O #{url}"` writes that unauthenticated response into the build tree. The return value of `system` is discarded, so a hostile, truncated, or resumed-against-a-modified-server fetch is indistinguishable from success; `wget -c` / `curl -C -` resume semantics additionally let a server append to a partial file.
tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:46 and :49 — the identical unauthenticated http:// fetch for the Windows `sqlitedll-<version>.zip`, i.e. the binary artifact, under the same missing-integrity conditions.

Guard checked and absent — greps for `checksum`, `sha1`, `sha256`, `gpg`, `signature`, and `verify` across the working tree and across all 260 commits (`git log --all -S'sha1'`, `-S'https://www.sqlite.org'`) return no hit for these tasks: no expected digest is pinned in the repository and https was never used, so nothing can compare the downloaded bytes against a trusted value.

tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:55-59 — the downloaded archive is declared as the prerequisite and extracted with `sh "unzip #{full_file}"` into vendor/sqlite3/include; there is no member-name filtering, no `-o`/`-d` confinement, and no path-traversal check, so archive member names chosen by the attacker are materialised as filesystem paths.

tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:61 — after extraction, `touch File.basename(t.name)` only stamps the expected file name so Rake will not repeat the task; it is not a verification step and it does not establish that the archive contained a genuine sqlite3.h.

tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:67-73 — the same extract-then-touch sequence materialises the attacker-supplied sqlite3.dll into vendor/sqlite3/lib, and tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:79-85 turns that DLL into the import library via dlltool.

tasks/native.rake:7,17,21 — `sqlite3_lib` is the vendor/sqlite3 directory and is passed to the extension build as `--with-sqlite3-dir=#{sqlite3_lib}` (and `cross_config_options` for cross builds), so the extracted headers and import library are handed to the compiler and linker as the SQLite3 dependency.

ext/sqlite3/extconf.rb:12,19,20 — `dir_config 'sqlite3'` consumes that directory, and the only checks are `find_header 'sqlite3.h'` and `find_library 'sqlite3', 'sqlite3_libversion_number'`: presence of a header and of one symbol. Neither check establishes authenticity, provenance, or a minimum version, so an attacker-authored header and library satisfy them.

ext/sqlite3/sqlite3_ruby.h:21 — `#include <sqlite3.h>` pulls the attacker-controlled header into ext/sqlite3/sqlite3.c, database.c, statement.c, and exception.c (each includes sqlite3_ruby.h at line 1), so arbitrary attacker C text (macros, declarations, static initialisers) becomes part of the compiled, published binary.

Reachability guard checked, and its limit — Rakefile at HEAD contains no `import`/`Dir['tasks/*.rake']` (that loader was removed in commit fb1c2b1, which is in HEAD's history) and there is no rakelib/ directory, so `vendor:sqlite3` is not wired into the default build at HEAD. The vulnerable file is nonetheless still shipped (Manifest.txt:32) and defines its tasks whenever it is loaded directly (it references no HOE constant, so it loads standalone, unlike tasks/native.rake:5); exploitation therefore requires the task to be invoked explicitly or the loader to be restored. I did not execute rake to confirm this, which is why confidence is MEDIUM.
preconditions: The vendoring task must be loaded and run — either by restoring the `Dir['tasks/*.rake']` import in the Rakefile, by invoking the file directly (for example `rake -f tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake vendor:sqlite3`), or on a Windows/cross-compile host where tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:100-105 unshifts vendor:sqlite3 onto the compile/cross prerequisites.
The vendor archives must not already be present and up to date in vendor/, since Rake skips the file tasks when the targets are newer than their prerequisites.

The attacker must hold an active network position on the path to www.sqlite.org for the duration of the download: hostile or shared Wi-Fi, a malicious/transparent proxy, ARP or DNS spoofing, a rogue CI egress node, BGP hijack, or control of a mirror/CDN edge. A purely passive eavesdropper is not sufficient.
For the supply-chain half of the impact, the poisoned build must be the one whose output is packaged and published (a maintainer release or cross-compile build), rather than a throwaway local build.
exploitScenarios: A maintainer or CI job starts a Windows/cross-compile build on a network the attacker can intercept, so vendor:sqlite3 runs as a prerequisite of compile/cross (tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:100-105).
The file task at tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:35 fires and line 36 constructs the plaintext URL http://www.sqlite.org/sqlite-amalgamation-3_6_16.zip.

Line 39 shells out to wget/curl; the attacker intercepts the unencrypted request and answers it with a zip of their own choosing, which no TLS handshake, checksum, or signature can detect, and whose failure would be silent anyway because the return value of `system` is discarded.
The attacker repeats the substitution for the second fetch at line 49 to control vendor/sqlite3/lib/sqlite3.dll, from which line 85 derives the import library.

The extraction task at tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake:55 runs `unzip` on the hostile archive (line 59) with no member filtering, dropping an attacker-authored sqlite3.h into vendor/sqlite3/include, and optionally writing additional members to paths outside vendor/ via traversal entries; the touch at line 61 then marks the task satisfied.

tasks/native.rake:17/:21 passes --with-sqlite3-dir at that vendor directory, and ext/sqlite3/extconf.rb:12,19,20 accepts it because a file named sqlite3.h exists and the sqlite3_libversion_number symbol resolves in the attacker's library.

make compiles ext/sqlite3/*.c, each of which reaches ext/sqlite3/sqlite3_ruby.h:21 and #includes the attacker's header, so the attacker's C executes at build time (and their library is linked in), giving code execution on the build host.
The resulting binary extension is packaged and published, so every user who installs the gem loads the attacker's code into their Ruby process.
recommendations: Root-cause fix: retrieve the archives over https:// with certificate verification enforced, and verify each downloaded file against a SHA-256 digest pinned in the repository before it is allowed to satisfy the file task or be extracted — abort the build on mismatch rather than proceeding.

Stop discarding the transfer result: replace `system "..."` with `sh` (which raises on non-zero status) or check the return value, and drop the resume flags (`wget -c`, `curl -C -`) so a partially written or server-appended file cannot be mistaken for a complete, verified download.

Hardening: extract with confinement and member validation — use `unzip -o -d <target>` and reject or strip any member whose normalised path escapes vendor/sqlite3/{include,lib} or is absolute, instead of trusting the archive's member names; then assert the expected files exist rather than using `touch` to fake task satisfaction.
Hardening: prefer a vendored-in-tree or package-manager-provided SQLite3 amalgamation over a network fetch during build, and quote interpolated paths passed to the shell in dlltool/unzip invocations.

Regression test: add a build-level test that points the download at a local server serving a deliberately corrupted archive (wrong digest, and one containing a `../` traversal member) and asserts that the vendor task fails loudly, writes nothing outside vendor/sqlite3, and never reaches the compile step.

I read the full component and its trigger path, then traced the single input source and every sink back to a trust boundary. My conclusion is **no reportable findings** for this component under the injection/input lens.

**What I verified**

- `faq/faq.rb:75` is the sole input: `YAML.load( File.read( "faq.yml" ) )` — no `safe_load`, no `permitted_classes`. The sink is genuinely dangerous in the abstract, but the "attacker-controlled source" is `faq/faq.yml`, a file in the same repository tree as `faq/faq.rb` itself. Anyone able to change `faq.yml` can change `faq.rb`, the `Rakefile`, or `lib/`, so deserialization grants no privilege the writer does not already have. There is no boundary crossing, only a code-equivalent data file.
- Reachability is dead. `tasks/faq.rake:5` defines the `faq` file task, but the current `Rakefile` (read in full, 32 lines) never imports `tasks/*.rake`, and there is no `rakelib/` directory that Rake would auto-load. `git log -S "tasks/*.rake" -- Rakefile` shows the import added in `d6e96ef` and **removed in `fb1c2b1`** ("initial start for custom c bindings", Jan 2010), never restored. So `rake faq` is an undefined task today; `tasks/native.rake` and `tasks/vendor_sqlite3.rake` are orphaned the same way. Nothing else in the tree — `setup.rb`, `ext/sqlite3/extconf.rb`, `lib/`, `test/` — references `faq`.
- No external content ever becomes `faq.yml`. A repo-wide search for `faq` finds only `tasks/faq.rake`, `Manifest.txt:17-18`, and the component itself. Nothing downloads, generates, or writes that file.
- The HTML sinks (`faq.rb:23`, `:46`–`:48`) do no escaping, and `add_api_links` rewrites already-rendered HTML including inside `<pre>` and attribute values. This is not exploitable as XSS: RedCloth's Textile intentionally passes raw HTML through, `faq.yml:9-14` relies on that with literal `<pre>` blocks, and the person supplying the markup is the document's own author. Injecting script into a page you author is not a privilege gain.
- `tasks/faq.rake:7` (`ruby "faq.rb > faq.html"`) does hand a shell metacharacter to a shell, but the command string is entirely static — no interpolation of any data — so there is no injection path.
- The regex at `faq.rb:60` interpolates `API_OBJECTS` (`faq.rb:52-57`), a static alternation of six literal class names followed by `(#(\w+))?`. No nested or overlapping quantifiers, so no catastrophic backtracking — not ReDoS.
- `File.read("faq.yml")` uses a static relative literal, so there is no attacker-controlled path component and no traversal.
- I searched `faq/`, `tasks/`, `Rakefile`, and `README.rdoc` for instruction-style text, non-ASCII/hidden characters, and YAML anchors/aliases/tags. `faq.yml` contains only ordinary FAQ prose, and no agent pipeline in the repo consumes it — no prompt-injection finding.

**Not checked:** I ran nothing. The Psych/RedCloth versions that would actually be resolved at build time are undetermined (no `Gemfile`, no `.gemspec`, no CI config exists in the tree, and `redcloth` is not even declared as a dependency), but that only affects the severity of a path I am already rejecting on trust-boundary and reachability grounds.

## What I read

`faq/faq.rb` (all 145 lines), `faq/faq.yml` (all 426 lines), `tasks/faq.rake` (all 9 lines), plus `Rakefile`, `Manifest.txt`, `lib/sqlite3.rb`, `ext/sqlite3/extconf.rb`, and the `setup.rb` hook machinery to test reachability, and git history via the read-only wrapper.

## Candidates traced and why each was rejected

**SSRF / open redirect at `faq/faq.rb:68`.** The threat model calls this a network boundary. The href is a hardcoded literal; the only interpolated values are `obj` and `method`, and `obj` can only be one of the six literal names built into `API_OBJECTS` at `faq/faq.rb:52-57` because it is a capture of that alternation, while `method` is constrained to `\w+` by `(#(\w+))?` at `faq/faq.rb:60`. No attacker-controlled bytes reach the URL. Nothing server-side fetches it, so it is neither SSRF nor a redirect.

**Open redirect / IDOR at `faq/faq.rb:23` and `faq/faq.rb:46`.** `question.object_id` is an Integer emitted into a same-document fragment. There is no resource identifier, no lookup, and no authorization decision to bypass.

**Privilege escalation via `YAML.load` at `faq/faq.rb:75`.** This is the one genuinely dangerous sink, but it does not cross a privilege boundary in this repository, so there is no escalation and no auth-category finding:

- The only trigger is `tasks/faq.rake:5-7`, invoked manually. There is no CI — `git log --all --diff-filter=A` over `.github`, `.travis.yml`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, and `appveyor.yml` returns nothing, so no automated principal ever runs it.
- Nothing loads `tasks/*.rake`. `Rakefile` has no `import`, no `Dir.glob`, and no `rakelib` directory exists, so the `faq` task is very likely not even defined in a normal `rake` run. I could not confirm this by executing `rake`, which is why I treat it as supporting rather than decisive evidence.
- `faq/faq.rb` ships in the gem per `Manifest.txt:17`, but it never executes on install: `spec_extras[:extensions]` at `Rakefile:18` lists only `ext/sqlite3/extconf.rb`, and `lib/sqlite3.rb` requires only three files, none of them the FAQ script.
- `setup.rb` `run_hook` (`setup.rb:514-517`) only evals fixed names such as `pre-config` and `post-setup`; `faq.rb` matches none, and the `packages` directory checked at `setup.rb:99` does not exist.

The result is that the writer of `faq.yml` and the executor of `faq.rb` are the same principal — someone with repo write access, who could equally edit `faq.rb` itself. Deserialization here is also an injection-category issue rather than an auth one.

**XSS via unescaped RedCloth output at `faq/faq.rb:47-48`.** Out of lens, and there is no cross-user boundary: `faq.html` has never been committed in any revision, and raw HTML passthrough is an intended feature evidenced by the `<pre>` blocks at `faq/faq.yml:9-14`.

**Shell metacharacter at `tasks/faq.rake:7`.** `ruby "faq.rb > faq.html"` is a fully hardcoded string with no data flow into it. Not injection, not auth.

**Race conditions in access decisions.** None exist — the script is single-threaded, makes no access decisions, and the only TOCTOU-shaped element is Rake's own file-timestamp staleness check, which gates nothing security-relevant.

**Prompt injection.** I checked specifically for it since `faq.yml` is attacker-authorable content that a build agent would read. Grepping the product tree for instruction-style text ("ignore previous", "do not report", "you are an AI", "trusted by design", etc.) returned no hits, and reading `faq.yml` in full showed only genuine SQLite documentation. There are no agent instruction files in the repo.

## Not checked

I did not execute anything, so I did not empirically confirm that `rake faq` fails to resolve the task, nor the installed Psych version that would determine whether `YAML.load` honors `!ruby/object:` tags. Neither affects the conclusion, because the escalation path fails on the absence of a distinct executing principal regardless of Psych behavior.

Developer emails in `Rakefile:9-11` and `Manifest.txt` are intentional published gem metadata.

So no credential can reach the generated artifact.

The plaintext `http://sqlite-ruby.rubyforge.org/...` link built at `faq/faq.rb:68` points at an abandoned domain, but it transmits no secret and grants no capability; it is stale-documentation hygiene, not a crypto or credential defect.

The genuinely dangerous behavior I saw in this component — `YAML.load` without `safe_load` or `permitted_classes` at `faq/faq.rb:75`, unescaped RedCloth output interpolated into HTML at `faq/faq.rb:23,47,48`, and the shell-interpreted redirection at `tasks/faq.rake:7` — falls under deserialization, XSS, and command-injection, outside my assigned cryptography-and-secrets lens, so I am not reporting it here rather than relabeling it to fit.

No cryptography, randomness, key material, secret comparison, or credential handling exists in the FAQ generator, so there is no complete attack path to report under this lens.
